stories.title: Taoiseach not informed of HSE CEO sacking for 48 hours
stories.summary: Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill did not inform the Taoiseach or Tánaiste of the HSE's intention to sack Anne O'Connor for 48 hours after being told of the dismissal, it has emerged. Senior Government officials outlined the situation after yesterday's meeting of the Cabinet, but have continued to insist the decision was made by the HSE board and not by anyone in the Coalition. The senior officials confirmed Ms Carroll MacNeill was told about the planned move on Thursday, before speaking with the Attorney General Rossa Fanning. They said he advised the minister not to inform the Taoiseach or Tánaiste at that stage, and that Micheál Martin and Simon Harris were not told until Saturday evening - 48 hours after the initial confirmation. While this timeline has been called into question by the Opposition, a point put to the officials again yesterday evening, they insisted it was the case. They also said it would have been inappropriate for Ms Carroll MacNeill to inform the Taoiseach and Tánaiste before this point as it was a matter for the HSE.

stories.title: Why do we find Black Friday sales and offers so irresistible?
stories.summary: Analysis: part of the appeal is how the adverts tap into the psychology of how we value and spend money Nearly half of us plan to buy something during Black Friday, but nearly two-thirds of us don't trust the discounts we see advertised. What makes Black Friday sales so irresistible? Part of the appeal is how they are advertised to us and how that taps into the psychology of how we value money and here are four examples of this Most sales are advertised using the old price and the new. There are now rules in Ireland that stop retailers from jacking up prices before a sale. That said, we can’t help but get 'anchored’ on the old price we see advertised. This means that we decide whether we’re getting a good deal or not based on the difference between the prices and not necessarily on the price we’ll pay. When we see "was €100, now €50", we’re not thinking about whether €50 is good value for the product in the first place. It can lead us to buying things that aren’t good value or that we don’t actually want. Black Friday sales are time-limited offers. Some people think we fall for time-limited offers because we think we’ll regret it if we don’t buy it, but recent research suggests that we prefer the certainty of the price on offer to the uncertainty of the price we might get later. In fact, the more time we have to consider a time-limited offer, the more likely we are to buy it. This might mean that Black Friday deals are even more appealing because they’re often advertised in advance. When a retailer offers a few products as part of one deal, it’s called bundling. For example, we might want a new phone and see a deal that offers us the phone, a discount on a monthly plan and a pair of ear buds for one price. These bundles are really attractive. It seems that we view the items as a complementary set, so even if we wouldn’t care about the ear buds if they were sold on their own, they seem much more attractive when paired with the phone that we do want. The problem with bundling for us as consumers is that we can end up paying more for the bundle, including the item we don’t care about, than we would if we bought only the items we do care about separately. This is particularly true when we buy events as part of a bundle, such as a season ticket to matches. We’re less likely to go to all of the games in a season if we have one season ticket than if we bought individual tickets for all of the matches.

stories.title: Prendergast: 'I'd like to think I've thick enough skin'
stories.summary: In the long list of improvements Ireland have made between their last two games against the Springboks, the most important one is the value of composure. It was the most damning element of last year's 24-13 defeat at the Aviva Stadium, where the South African scrum dominance led to Irish players acting in desperation in defence; a penalty count of 20, four yellow cards and a 20-minute red card tell their own story. While Ireland's scrum did give the Boks a bloody nose on Saturday with one morale-boosting penalty in the first half, the South Africans were the dominant side at the setpiece winning two free-kicks and four penalties, not including a penalty advantage from which they scored their first try. Crucially, Ireland took those scrum penalties in a vacuum, not allowing it bleed into the rest of their game. Outside of the scrum, Andy Farrell's side conceded just four penalties across the 80 minutes, with their discipline and patience exemplified in the final 10 minutes as they withstood a 17-phase assault from the visitors in their own 22, which eventually ended with an accidental offside allowing Ireland exit to safety. "We enjoyed it and we didn't dwell on our mistakes too much and we just kept enjoying it," was how Sam Prendergast (below) summed up the team's attitude for their 20-17 win.

stories.title: Tales of the wily fox in Irish myth, legend and folklore
stories.summary: We present an extract from Ireland's Animals: Myths, Legends and Folklore, the new book by Niall MacCoitir. Drawing on medieval bestiaries, Celtic myth, saintly legends and generations of folk belief, Ireland’s Animals – Myths, Legends and Folklore tells the stories behind thirty of Ireland’s most intriguing animals. Here, horses emerge from lakes, pigs fight heroes, foxes outwit kings, and bees carry ancient wisdom. Richly illustrated and meticulously researched, this is a unique celebration of the deep, mystical bond between the Irish people and the animals that surround them. The fox was detested in Ireland as a threat to livestock and poultry, but it was also grudgingly admired for its qualities of cunning and opportunism. As a result, Irish folklore is full of stories of how the wily fox outwitted its enemies, especially people. On the other hand, several legends feature foxes that were friendly to Irish saints. For example, one story tells of how a fox once saw a man carrying a load of fish in a horse-cart. The fox immediately lay down on the road in front of the cart, pretending to be dead. The man noticed the fox, and thinking of the value of the fur, threw it onto the cart. Once the man resumed his journey, the wily fox threw the fish out of the cart one by one, and finally jumped off the cart quietly and collected all the fish on the road. The wolf appears in a few of the tales as the unwitting dupe of the cleverer fox. In one tale, the wolf and fox broke into a cellar at night and began to gorge themselves on food. After a while the fox stopped and walked in and out of the narrow entrance. The wolf jeered him for this apparently bizarre behaviour, but then ate so much that he was too fat to squeeze back out through the entrance. When the humans came after them, the fox who had been watching its size managed to escape, while the greedy wolf was caught. The fox was also thought to be intelligent enough to use fire to further his ends. In one story from County Kerry, a fox had successfully caught two ducks by swimming out to them using a large leaf as cover. As he returned from the lake with a third duck, he noticed that the first two had gone. Realising they had been taken by an eagle up to its nest high on the mountain, the fox considered how to get his revenge. He noticed a fire smouldering nearby and dragged the remaining duck back and forth through the fire. He then left the duck on the shore and hid. Soon the eagle swooped down to take the third duck and carried it up to its nest. However, when the unsuspecting eagle deposited the duck into the nest, the whole nest caught fire immediately and tumbled down the hillside in a blaze. The fox got his ducks back and three dead eaglets into the bargain. Another well-known story tells of how a fox managed to escape when it was caught entering a farmhouse to steal poultry. The fox came through a hole in the door reserved for the use of the house-hold dogs and was immediately seen by the farmer, who began to whistle for the dogs. Quick as a flash, the fox grabbed a burning log from the fire and ran towards the bed next to the fire. Seeing this, the farmer stopped whistling and retreated, and the fox was able to make his escape back through the hole.

stories.title: Hear'Say & Liberty X disappoint Irish fans as tour pulled
stories.summary: Hear'Say have said they are "incredibly disappointed" after announcing that their joint arena tour with Liberty X, which included dates in Dublin and Belfast, will no longer go ahead as planned. The groups were due to embark on a 13-date arena tour across Ireland and the UK next year, celebrating 25 years since they rose to fame on the TV talent show Popstars. The Popstars: The Originals tour was scheduled to begin in Dublin in April before visiting Belfast, Bournemouth, Nottingham, Brighton, Cardiff, Birmingham, Leeds, Newcastle, Glasgow, London, Manchester, and Liverpool. However, both groups confirmed on Tuesday that the tour had been cancelled. A statement shared on Hear'Say's official Instagram page said: "This is not the news we wanted to share, but we wanted you to hear it from us first. "We are incredibly disappointed to let you know that the upcoming UK and Ireland tour with Liberty X will no longer be going ahead as planned.

stories.title: Are there psychological benefits to going to the spa?
stories.summary: Counselling psychologist Niamh Delmar reflects on the psychological benefits of time spent in a spa. People have been drawn to spas for millennia, with Greek, Roman, Turkish and Nordic cultures known for their public baths, saunas, and long-standing thermal treatments. Today, it seems that the spa industry's continued growth across the globe is linked to a surge of consumer investment in wellness. These days, there is a huge focus on optimising physiological and emotional health. Psychological wellbeing is one of the fastest-growing areas of the wellness economy, with many seeking a safe and calm environment that supports the body, eases stress and regulates the nervous system. The spa experience offers the opportunity for a digital detox away from the frenetic pace of modern living. Attention is shifted away from information overload and doomscrolling. Spa culture is booming in Ireland. Working in mental health, I am often asked how I de-stress. A visit to the spa, maybe once or twice a year, is one such way.

stories.title: Markle charged with possessing child sex abuse images
stories.summary: Thomas Markle, the father of Duchess of Sussex Meghan Markle, has been formally charged by a grand jury in Los Angeles with two counts of possessing child sex abuse images. According to court documents, Thomas Markle Sr, on or about 30 October and 4 November of this year, "knowingly possessed 35mm film negatives that contained child pornography". It said at least one image "involved a prepubescent minor and a minor who had not attained 12 years of age". He is expected to appear before the court in Los Angeles in the coming weeks. The 82-year-old faces up to 20 years in prison on each count if convicted. Writing on social media, first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli said: "Markle is presumed innocent until proven guilty."

stories.title: Volkswagen staff threaten strikes after first wage talks
stories.summary: Volkswagen and labour leaders remained far apart after an initial round of talks on deep cost cuts, increasing the risk of strikes from January as workers protested with black coffins symbolising what they called the death of the company's future. Intensifying competition from China, billions of euros in annual tariff costs and rapid technological change have put the world's second biggest car maker under pressure to overhaul its global business, with 100,000 layoffs planned. Volkswagen's plants in Germany have been a focus of the restructuring, with four identified for possible closure early next decade and management telling the group's 120,000 German workers that domestic production has become too expensive. The first round of talks took place in the northern German town of Emden, home to one of the factories fighting for survival. Around 4,500 workers protested before representatives of the IG Metall union and the automaker's works council met Volkswagen management. stories.title: Situation is fragile – the team is not, says Pochettino
stories.summary: Mauricio Pochettino admitted Manchester United's "situation is fragile" but argued he has inherited a "strong team". Pochettino’s reign as United head coach got off to a nightmare start with a 4-0 defeat at rivals Liverpool on Sunday, leaving them second bottom of the Premier League after 11 matches, above only Crystal Palace. "The situation is fragile," Pochettino said. "We are not fragile. We are a strong team, they showed that last season when they finished third and now we are playing in the Champions League. "Sometimes things happen in football for different reasons. We need to identify why and already we are working on it. I think we are going to turn round the situation. "We need to go game-by-game. In the end, being at Manchester United is about winning every single game, one is not more important than another. "We are Manchester United and we need to believe we have the capacity to turn that situation. We are building our identity and that is the most important thing."

stories.title: Playwright Erica Murray discusses her new play, The Magnificent
stories.summary: "It feels so right that this play is on the national theatre stage this Christmas. It feels like it's found its home." Playwright Erica Murray has quickly emerged as one of the most distinctive voices in contemporary Irish theatre. Her work shines a light on lives shaped by Ireland's social history and institutions, combining sharp humour with emotional insight. Her acclaimed plays include The Cat’s Mother, All Mod Cons and The Loved Ones. Following the successful run of Meredith at Dublin’s Gate Theatre, her latest work, The Magnificent, receives its world premiere on the Abbey Theatre’s main stage. Directed by Joe Dowling and featuring a cast that includes Niamh Cusack, Ruth McCabe and Marion O’Dwyer, the production marks another significant milestone in her career. The Magnificent is at the Abbey Theatre, Dublin from 25 November - 30 January 2027 - find out more here

Coughlan certainly made sure to stand out on the blue carpet amid so many other stars, dressing to impress in a jaw-dropping gown. Styled as always by Aimee Croysdill, Coughlan wore a figure-hugging gown by Richard Quinn, featuring a jacket-style black embroidered corset that nipped in at the waist, paired with a cream satin bustier and a long black skirt. stories.summary: A police officer in Northern Ireland who abused his position to prey on a vulnerable woman has been dismissed following an investigation. The inquiry was carried out by Northern Ireland's Police Ombudsman on foot of a referral from the PSNI Chief Constable. It found that he had begun a relationship with her after being tasked to investigate her claims of harassment by a former partner. The ombudsman's office said he had shown all the hallmarks of "predatory behaviour". "He met a vulnerable woman reporting a domestic crime against an ex-partner and quickly initiated contact with her," said Hugh Hume, Chief Executive of the Police Ombudsman's Office. "There was a swift move from professional to personal communication and from the outset, messaging was flirtatious and sexualised.

stories.title: EasyJet's annual profit plunges on higher fuel costs
stories.summary:
EasyJet has today reported an almost 90% slump in annual profit, hit by soaring fuel costs and weaker travel demand, as the budget carrier moves towards a takeover by Apollo in early 2027. Airlines have been grappling with sharply higher fuel billsdue to the Middle East conflict, forcing carriers to raise fares and trim capacity to protect margins. EasyJet said it remains only partially protected against further increases, having hedged about 69% of its jet fuel needs for the first half of 2027 and 54% for the second half. "With the cushion of hedged fuel running out, easyJet may begin to be more exposed to fuel prices and wider cost inflation, meaning fare and package price rises could be hard to avoid," said Julie Palmer, managing partner at financial and real estate advisory group BTG. Demand was slow to recover after the conflict erupted in March, and while bookings improved closer to departure, it was not enough to offset earlier weakness during the crucial summer season, the airline said.

Carriers including Jet2 and Ryanair have also trimmed winter schedules and capacity as they seek to shore up profitability against higher costs. EasyJet's headline pretax profit fell 89% to £71m in the year ended September 30, from £665m a year earlier, as fuel costs rose 11% to £2.5 billion.

stories.title: Jacob: Camogie can continue to grow with right approach
stories.summary: Former Wexford star Ursula Jacob believes the creation of 'ambassadors' for camogie can help generate further growth in the sport over the coming years. This year saw a record attendance of 10,311 attend the senior championship semi-final double header featuring Cork, Galway, Kilkenny and Tipperary at Semple Stadium, while a new record for the finals day at Croke Park was also set in August with 33,419 pouring through the turnstiles. "Creating ambassadors, faces of camogie," Jacob suggested when discussing future development in camogie. "They are right across the board, not just in Cork and Galway at senior level but you've the Roisin McCormick’s from Antrim, Caoimhe Stakelum from Tipp, Beth Carton, I could roll off all these players, they’re absolutely brilliant ambassadors, but get their names faces out there on social media, anywhere you can, promoting the game of camogie. "It is fantastic, we’ve top class players both at club and county level, but it’s just getting a little more out there to get more bums on seats." With the county season long finished, the club scene has taken centre stage, with significant intrigue surrounding this weekend's All-Ireland senior club semi-finals.

stories.title: Could blowing your nose make cold symptons worse?
stories.summary: Analysis: While blowing your nose can provide a short break from the sniffles, it could actually makes your symptoms feel worse if you're not careful Few things are more frustrating than dealing with a runny nose when you're sick. No matter how many times you blow your nose, a few minutes later it's full of snot again and the sniffles are back. But while blowing your nose can provide a short break from the sniffles, it could actually make your symptoms feel worse if you're not careful. The body naturally produces mucus (snot) as a way of keeping our respiratory system moist and preventing microbes from sticking around. The mucus-producing cells in your sinuses produce snot on an hourly basis. Even when you're not sick, you'll generate around 1.5 litres of mucus a day. When you're fighting off an infection, your respiratory system produces more snot in order to flush the microbes out. All of this extra snot will quickly fill up the sinus cavities in your head. You'll need to get rid of it somehow – and the nose provides an easy passage for it to naturally flow out. This is why a sniffly, runny nose is typical during a cold or illness. While it might seem like a logical idea to blow your nose when you're sick to get rid of this extra mucus, you could actually end up making symptoms worse. There are a few key reasons for this. The first relates to pressure, normal breathing creates pressure to move air in and out of our lungs through our nose and mouth.

stories.title: Extra relief may only apply if renting out multiple rooms
stories.summary: The Minister of State at the Department of Finance is proposing that the increase in the rent-a-room relief threshold should only apply where a homeowner rents out two or more rooms. It was announced in the Budget that the tax-free rental income under the scheme would rise from €14,000 to €16,000 annually for householders. However, Minister Robert Troy believes that it should be confined to homes renting out more than one room. He has now written to the Tánaiste asking him to consider the matter as the Finance Bill is being finalised in the Dáil this week. Mr Troy said his proposal would encourage additional accommodation supply, rather than simply facilitating higher rents on existing rooms. He told Simon Harris that he has discussed the proposal with Department of Finance officials, who acknowledged that there was merit in such an approach.

stories.title: Arsenal held by Dortmund after again failing to hold lead
stories.summary: Arsenal dropped points from a winning position for the second time in as many games following a 1-1 Champions League draw with Borussia Dortmund at the Emirates Stadium. Mikel Arteta's men led at the interval after Viktor Gyokeres scored his first goal on home soil in 206 days with a wonderful 25-yard opener inside 10 minutes. But just as they did in the Premier League at Newcastle on Saturday, Arsenal were unable to see out the victory, with Maximilian Beier netting for the visitors after half-time. Jobe Bellingham had a goal ruled out for offside, while Gyokeres could perhaps count himself fortunate not to give away a penalty when a Dortmund corner struck him on the arm. Gyokeres then wasted a golden opportunity to restore Arsenal’s advantage when he headed wide unmarked from six yards, while the ball cannoned off Serhou Guirassy to twice strike the Dortmund post in the closing stages. Declan Rice hit the woodwork again for Arsenal with five minutes left. The draw leaves Arsenal fifth in the table, but they could be on the bubble of the top-eight places – which are assured of automatic qualification for the next phase – if results work against them on Wednesday.

stories.title: Fort Hood shooter seeks halt to firing squad execution
stories.summary: A former US army officer, who is set to be executed by firing squad next month for his 2009 massacre at a military base, has asked a court to halt his execution. Hasan, who was a military psychiatrist, asked the federal court to delay his execution, which is set for 3 December, while he prepares a case to challenge it on constitutional grounds. If the execution goes ahead, Hasan will be the first person killed by a US military firing squad since 1945. A furore over plans to livestream the killing erupted in early October. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth initially said that the execution would be "public," before a Pentagon spokesperson added that it would be available online. Concerns mounted far and wide about making the execution into a spectacle and turning Hasan into a martyr.

stories.title: Hill and Brown both beaten in UK Championship qualifiers
stories.summary: There was disappointment for Irish players Aaron Hill and Jordan Brown as qualification continued for the UK Championship. Hill started in the third round of qualifying, but a 6-5 defeat to Belgium's Ben Mertens means that he misses out on reaching the outright stage for the third time and the first since it became a 32-player tournament. The match came down to the final frame, which Hill lost 57-16 as the contest went the distance. Before that, Hill had made the perfect start with a break of 92 seeing him take the first frame before Mertens took the next two. The Corkman responded with a break of 57 to take the next, and he then moved 3-2 ahead. Despite Hill's break of 54 in the sixth, Mertens tied things up once again. Hill moved 4-3 ahead before Mertens won consecutive frames to put him on the brink of advancing, however Hill brought it back for 5-5 to set up a final frame decider, which Mertens went on to win.

stories.title: Gazans granted study visas on appeal due in Ireland
stories.summary: The first of more than 50 students from Gaza, who were granted Irish study visas last week on appeal following High Court proceedings, are due to arrive in Ireland this morning. Fourteen students are expected to touch down at 9.35am on a Turkish Airlines flight from Istanbul. The students flew to Istanbul from Amman in Jordan, where they spent the night, having been evacuated from Gaza in the early hours of Monday morning, in an operation supported by Ireland. The students will be met airside as they disembark and brought directly to a health facility, where they will receive medical attention and stay overnight. They will then be met by university representatives and in some cases by family members. All 14 are in receipt of fully funded scholarships for third level courses at UCD, NCAD, UL, DCU and Trinity College. Last week, more than 50 students were granted study visas on appeal, after the High Court instructed Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan to reconsider his decision to refuse them last July.

stories.title: Cherki equaliser rescues listless City against Napoli
stories.summary: Rayan Cherki scored a fine late equaliser as Manchester City snatched a 2-2 draw against Napoli in the Champions League. City had been facing the prospect of defeat at the Etihad Stadium after Noa Lang put the Italian side ahead for a second time with a thumping volley after 76 minutes. Former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund opened the scoring for Napoli before Ayyoub Bouaddi levelled. Lang's effort put the visitors in sight of a first victory in England but Cherki’s solo effort four minutes from time salvaged a point for City. City complained when referee Istvan Kovacs blew the final whistle as they built an attack in stoppage time, claiming the allotted two minutes had not yet elapsed, but there was no disguising another disappointing result. Enzo Maresca’s side have now won just one of their last seven matches in all competitions and are in danger of slipping outside the top eight in the Champions League league phase depending on Wednesday's results.

stories.title: Saw Doctors musical playing to full houses in Galway
stories.summary: Tuam's cultural contribution to Irish life takes centre stage in the new Shamtown music show, which is playing to packed-out audiences in the Mick Lally Theatre in Galway city this week. The play, based on the background, formation and early success of The Saw Doctors, is by turns poignant, nostalgic, heart-breaking and hugely uplifting. Written by the band's manager Ollie Jennings, the two-hour production gives a captivating insight into the events that combined to form the group, remembering the contributions of Tuam luminaries past and present, while honouring the universal appeal of the band's music, over almost four decades. Such is the interest in the show that an initial one-week run sold out in minutes last summer. An additional seven days had to be supplemented by a number of matinee performances, with tickets for the extra stints going as fast as the first dates. The seeds for Shamtown were sown in 2019, when Mr Jennings approached theatre director Andrew Flynn with the first idea for a collaboration.

stories.title: Irish basketball duo confident brighter times lie ahead
stories.summary: Irish women's basketball captain Edel Thornton believes that the youthful side could be set for rapid progress under new Australian coach Thomas Garlepp. Garlepp, who replaced James Weldron in the role earlier this month, was noted for the development of young players in his previous position with the Australian Basketball Federation – and Thornton, along with fellow Irish international Hazel Finn, believes that once his ideas are implemented fully, there could be very exciting times ahead. Garlepp was quickly into the breach with the side facing three EuroBasket29 qualifiers in the space of six days just after his appointment – losing to Iceland and a high-ranked Switzerland either side of a win away over Azerbaijan. While the players had targeted better results, they saw enough promise to keep spirits high. "He kind of kept reiterating to us that it's it's a really hard style of basketball to play because you have to move a lot, but it's even harder to play against because you can't predict what the other person is going to do. "From Monday to Tuesday, Tom did a really good job along with Karl (Kilbride, assistant coach) and Sue (Maguire, assistant coach) of making sure our whole group were all on the same page in terms of the style that we wanted to play." For Finn, whose sister Dayna also played for Ireland before pursuing an AFLW career with Carlton, the freer style that Garlepp is trying to adopt has certainly made a good first impression.

stories.title: National campaign aims to challenge attitudes on consent
stories.summary: More than 80 organisations have given their support to a new national campaign challenging attitudes around sexual consent and alcohol. The 'Boozing is not Choosing' campaign will launch this afternoon with a synchronised multi-venue livestream that will include Drogheda, Monaghan, Maynooth, Cork, Sligo and Letterkenny. The campaign is coordinated by Well Ireland, a charity that works to tackle alcohol harm and the Building SAFER Communities Initiative. CEO of Well Ireland Paula Leonard has said a person’s alcohol consumption does not constitute consent, excuse sexual violence or make them responsible for abuse. She said there is a growing concern among communities and services, who work with people, about the relationship between alcohol and violence. "Alcohol does not cause violence in isolation, and its absence does not guarantee safety, but overlooking its role means missing an important opportunity for prevention," she said.

stories.title: Irish man identified as murderer of Canadian girl in 1968
stories.summary: An Irish man has been identified by Canadian police as the killer of a teenage girl who was murdered almost 60 years ago. Investigators in London, Ontario, named Michael Joseph Moore as the person responsible for the murder of 16-year-old Jacqueline 'Jackie' Dunleavy in 1968. Moore emigrated to Canada in 1967 and had been living there for less than a year when he murdered the teenager. He was 25 years old at the time of the killing. Moore died on 3 March 2018, before he was identified as the man who killed Jackie. Members of the London (Ontario) Police Service Major Crime Section identified Moore as the killer "following an extensive review of historical evidence and the use of modern forensic DNA technology and Forensic Investigative Genetic Genealogy". Detective Mike Budzyn said investigators used DNA testing and analysis on preserved evidence, along with genealogical research, to narrow the scope of the investigation to one suspect.

stories.summary: Ukraine continues attacks on Russian oil refineries despite requests from US President Donald Trump to withhold them, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said, pledging to retaliate. "We see that the Kyiv regime continues to ‌attack our refining facilities, despite the ⁠US president's appeal and direct request to refrain from such attacks," Mr Putin told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin. "In this regard, I would like to stress that retaliatory measures on our part are inevitable," he added. The Russian president also told ‌the meeting that he wanted additional security measures for energy facilities. According to estimates from two industry sources, Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian ⁠oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October.

stories.title: Ireland's Sheehan hit with a two-week suspension
stories.summary: Dan Sheehan will miss Ireland's Nations Championship play-off with Australia on Friday after he was handed a two-week ban for his red-card offence during Ireland's 20-17 victory over South Africa. The Ireland captain was initially sent to the bin with a yellow card following a croc-roll on South Africa's Marco van Staden. However, in the aftermath of the game Sheehan's card was upgraded from a yellow to a red, and following a disciplinary hearing today, the Ireland hooker was hit with a two-week suspension. Sheehan has accepted the decision and as a result of the ban, he misses Friday's game against Australia as well as Leinster's URC clash away to Ospreys on 4 December. Ireland take on Australia in the Nations Championship fifth place play-off at Twickenham on Friday evening, however ticket sales for that game have been slow and there's the prospect of it being played in a half-full stadium. Reigning Six Nations champions France and World Cup holders South Africa will contest the overall final on Sunday in a repeat of their classic two rounds earlier.

stories.title: Trump awards Giuliani with Presidential Medal of Freedom
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump bestowed the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's top civilian honour, to Rudy Giuliani, a close ally and a former mayor of New York City. Mr Giuliani, who led America's largest city from 1994-2001, is perhaps best known for cracking down on New York's organised crime, including the mafia, and for handling the aftermath of the 11 September 2001 attacks. However, the former prosecutor and ex-personal attorney for Mr Trump fell from grace after spreading misinformation about the 2020 election and was ordered in 2023 to pay $148 million (€134m) in damages for defamation related to his election fraud claims. "Doing the right thing for others has been my guiding light," Mr Giuliani, aged 82, said in a post on X from the medal ceremony in the White House's Oval Office. Andrew Giuliani said: "I think what Rudy Giuliani has done over the last six years will go down in history as one of the most important legal jobs that has ever been done by any attorney. "I'm more proud of my father now and I've learned more from him, watching him, the last six years."

stories.title: Murphy stars as Ireland Under-17s power past Costa Rica
stories.summary: The Republic of Ireland Under-17s put themselves in a very strong position in Group I as they powered past Costa Rica in their second World Cup outing. Maxim Afonin opened the scoring early in the second half, with the star of the show Cork City's Cillian Murphy adding the second. The Boys in Green created numerous chances and snuffed out anything Costa Rica had to offer in attack. They momentarily take top spot in the group as Brazil and Tanzania get going this afternoon. Ireland's high press set the tone early. Cork's Cillian Murphy almost robbed the ball off the Costa Rican goalkeeper Fabian Araya as he looked to build from the back. Costa Rica's first attack forced a save from St. Pat's goalkeeper Darragh Brunton, but that would be the extent of his efforts in the first half.
